source.title: Interpretable and Steerable Concept Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Akshay R. Kulkarni; T. Weng; V. Narayanaswamy; Shu-Sen Liu; W. Sakla; Kowshik Thopalli

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders as a framework for interpreting and steering vision representations, but it does not test whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs or whether those mixtures arise from superposition.
record.gate_note: The study measures CLIP-Dissect interpretability and downstream steerability, then divides SAE neurons into score-based groups. These are related to neuron interpretability but do not directly measure polysemanticity or test whether a neuron’s different responses share a feature. Concept-coverage results are about whether concepts appear in the SAE, not whether neurons have unrelated responses. Rows below record the reported neuron-group measurements as related findings, not as tests of a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates SAE latents (not model neurons) on vision encoders with CLIP-Dissect interpretability and steering scores, then proposes CB-SAE. It assumes base activations are polysemantic and never measures how many model neurons respond to unrelated inputs, or why. The only base-neuron number is a mean steerability score (0.173) for CLIP layer-22 neurons, which is not a polysemanticity rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that most vision SAE latents have low interpretability, low steerability or both. Only about 12–20% are high on both (29% under the null threshold). The SAE also misses 27–45% of ImageNet-related concepts. They propose CB-SAE, which prunes low-utility latents and adds a concept bottleneck, reporting +32.1% interpretability and +14.5% steerability.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates a post-hoc concept-bottleneck SAE framework; it does not reproduce the original sources’ method for identifying polysemantic neurons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported proportions of high/low interpretability and steerability groups change when the steerability threshold is changed from the SAE mean (0.232) to the original model-neuron null baseline (0.173). The groups also differ across the tested downstream models. The paper reports that interpretability scores for SAE and CB-SAE are consistently ordered across several CLIP-like evaluation models.

fits_no_version.finding: In vision SAEs with 65,536 latents, 12–20% of latents score above the mean on both CLIP-Dissect interpretability and steering. 30–36% score below the mean on both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many vision SAE latents are neither interpretable nor steerable by score-based metrics, and the proportions depend on the downstream model.

fits_no_version.finding: Using a null steerability threshold (0.173) instead of the mean (0.232) raises the high/high share from 18.84% to 29.14%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Estimated shares of useful SAE latents depend on the classification threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning latents by score and adding concept-bottleneck neurons raises average CLIP-Dissect and steering scores.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Score-based pruning plus supervised concept neurons improves SAE interpretability and steerability metrics.

record.problems: The core neuron-group results use score thresholds based on means, and the paper shows that an alternative steerability threshold changes the proportions substantially. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these group proportions. The paper acknowledges that its results depend on the reliability of CLIP-Dissect concept assignments. The reported metrics do not directly test whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 1 CB-SAE versus SAE averages and further CB-SAE ablation/sensitivity results because they evaluate proposed training changes, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Also omitted concept-set coverage counts and cited results from prior work because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Does not test whether vision-model neurons respond to several unrelated inputs; analyses SAE latents only.
Does not study language-model MLP neurons.
Does not test superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Does not study initialization, regularization or noise as causes under sufficient capacity.
Compares SAE types (Table 3), not the share of polysemantic neurons in the base model's architecture.
Does not reexamine canonical polysemantic neurons.
Threshold and CLIP-model sensitivity apply to SAE interpretability scores, not to polysemanticity judgments of model neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The paper mentions polysemantic activations only as motivation for using SAEs. Its subjects are SAE latents, so none of the claim's versions are tested, and none of the original sources' methods are reproduced.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether vision-model neurons respond strongly to several unrelated inputs or inspect the cited neuron example.
Studies vision encoders and downstream vision-language models, not polysemanticity in transformer-language-model MLP neurons.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse features being packed together under capacity pressure.
Does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Compares SAE variants and downstream systems on interpretability and steerability metrics, not the share of polysemantic neurons or its relation to performance.
Does not examine whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a common feature or whether improved tools reveal coherent jobs.
Varies score thresholds and evaluation models for interpretability/steerability, but does not test how activation-range sampling or explanation scoring changes a polysemanticity judgment.
